extracted.intended_audience: federal agency NEPA practitioners and decisionmakers preparing EISs and related NEPA documents
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance on preparing Environmental Impact Statements (EISs) under NEPA, including timing, format, content, supplementation/reevaluation, page limits, summaries, purpose and need, and alternatives analysis. Intended to guide agency procedures and document preparation to meet statutory and CEQ regulatory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start of NEPA process / timing of EIS
rubrics_metrics.description: Revise §1502.5(a) to refer to the feasibility analysis or equivalent stage evaluating whether to proceed with the project; agencies often begin 'pre-NEPA' work before issuing a NOI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ recognizes feasibility analyses are not a component for every agency; agencies should integrate NEPA into planning and decision-making and may begin pre-NEPA work before a formal NOI in order to meet NOI content requirements. CEQ declines to delineate additional phases in regulations because agencies have decades of experience implementing this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commencement after complete application (optional earlier coordination)
rubrics_metrics.description: §1502.5(b) clarifies agencies must begin preparing an EIS after receiving a complete application, though agencies can elect to begin the process earlier if they choose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ added 'complete' to paragraph (b) and encourages early conversations and coordination among Federal agencies, applicants, and other interested entities to improve efficiencies. CEQ declined to impose uniform deadlines (e.g., 30 days completeness decision, 6 months NOI) because regulations must apply across diverse agencies and contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: EIS page limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Align §1502.7 with NEPA section 107(e): EIS page limits are 150 pages, or 300 pages for proposals of extraordinary complexity, not including citations or appendices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ removed authority for senior agency official to authorize exceedances (statute provides no mechanism). Agencies are expected to meet page limits while fully considering statutory elements. CEQ encourages concise, readable documents and offers ways to comply (appendices, summaries, visual aids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of appendices for technical analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider placing technical analyses in appendices and summarizing them in plain language in the EIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendices (and citations) are excluded from the page count. This facilitates meeting page limits while preserving comprehensiveness. CEQ also suggests making EISs and technical appendices machine readable where feasible to facilitate data sharing and reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of visual aids and charts
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage use of visual aids, maps, drawings, charts, graphs, tables, interactive documents, insets, colors, and highlights to draw attention to key information and conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual aids are excluded from the definition of 'page' provided by §1508.1(bb). Visual aids and charts must be understandable to decision makers and the public, including non-technical audiences. CEQ did not add extra regulatory text because the stated purpose of visual aids is to enable ready understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing in plain language
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ regulations require EISs to be written in plain language to prepare readable, concise, and informative documents (§1502.8 and related).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ amended language from 'may' to 'should' in parts to encourage (not merely allow) use of plain language and visual aids; the plain-language requirement also applies to visual aids and charts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft EIS must meet final EIS requirements; agency adequacy determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft EISs must meet the requirements for final EISs; add phrase 'the agency determines that' to clarify that the agency preparing a draft EIS determines whether a draft is so inadequate as to preclude meaningful analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ deleted overly restrictive clauses and clarified agency responsibility for assessing draft adequacy. Agencies should coordinate with cooperating agencies on development of proposed action and range of alternatives as governed by §§1501.7 and 1501.8.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final EIS must consider and respond to comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Final EISs should 'consider and respond' to comments rather than merely 'address' them, restoring the 1978 language and aligning with §1503.4(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strengthens the standard for responding to public and agency comments. Agencies must identify and respond to relevant comment themes, not merely document receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of opposing views in final EIS
rubrics_metrics.description: Final EISs should discuss 'responsible opposing view' (CEQ retains the longstanding term).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ interprets 'responsible' to mean an opposing view with a reasoned basis (not arbitrary). CEQ declined to change the term to 'relevant and non-frivolous' because 'responsible' has longstanding regulatory usage and has not caused confusion in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to prepare a supplemental EIS (supplementation standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must consider a supplemental EIS when a major Federal action 'is incomplete or ongoing' and there are changes that may require supplementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ revised 'remains to occur' to 'is incomplete or ongoing' for clarity. Agencies should continue to focus on whether a change to the proposed action could have environmental effects not analyzed in the existing EIS when determining the need for supplementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triggers for supplementation — 'substantial new circumstances or information'
rubrics_metrics.description: §1502.9(d)(1)(ii) replaces 'significant' with 'substantial' and 'impacts' with 'effects' and adds 'substantial or important new circumstances or information' for consistency with section 108(1) of NEPA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ follows statutory language (42 U.S.C. 4336b(1)) and considers this consistent with longstanding practice. CEQ declined to add precise definitions for 'substantial' or 'important' because agencies have experience applying the supplementation standard and definitions are unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of supplementation (not limited to environmental effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes to purpose and need or alternatives that change could be relevant to supplementation, but CEQ notes scenarios where other criteria cover this and directs agencies to focus on whether changes create un-analyzed environmental effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ declined to expand paragraph (d)(1)(ii) to explicitly include changes to purpose/need or alternatives because such scenarios are addressed by other criteria; agencies should evaluate if changes cause environmental effects not previously analyzed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reevaluation as separate tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Redesignate prior paragraph as 'Reevaluation' to clarify that reevaluation is a separate tool to document new information when supplementation is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may reevaluate EISs to determine that supplementation is not required, to document why changes or new information are not 'substantial,' or to conduct additional analysis to determine whether supplementation is required. Agencies may also prepare a supplemental EA and FONSI to reevaluate an EIS; agencies have discretion over reevaluation timing for non-programmatic documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended EIS format and required sections
rubrics_metrics.description: §1502.10 revises the recommended format of an EIS, moves appendices and certain items (scoping summary, list of preparers) to appendices, and requires agencies to include all referenced sections if using a different format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ declines to require EIS format for EAs (§1501.5 addresses EA required sections). Agencies choosing an alternate format must still include the substantive sections referenced in paragraph (a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: §1502.11(a)–(g): the EIS cover should list 'lead, joint lead, and any cooperating agencies' to the extent feasible; include unique identification number from the NOI on the cover; do not require estimated preparation cost on the cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ allows omission of listing every cooperating agency when impracticable (may include a note indicating where cooperating agencies are listed). CEQ removed the requirement to include estimated preparation cost because of administrative burden, inconsistent methodologies, and limited utility; agencies may include cost information in appendices if they choose and should track costs internally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary content and format
rubrics_metrics.description: §1502.12: the summary should provide a clear, high-level overview of the proposed action and alternatives, the significant effects, and other critical information; summarize 'any disputed issues,' 'any issues to be resolved,' and 'key differences among alternatives'; identify the environmentally preferable alternative or alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ requires summaries be written in plain language and encourages visual aids and charts understandable to non-technical audiences. CEQ removed the mandatory 15-page limit and now encourages summaries not exceed 15 pages while allowing flexibility for more complex actions; summaries count toward the EIS page limits so agencies have incentive to be concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and need statement requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: §1502.13: revise to align with section 107(d) of NEPA requiring an EIS to include a statement that briefly summarizes the underlying purpose and need for the proposed agency action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ declines to restore the 2020 language requiring purpose and need to be based on applicant goals when an agency is reviewing an application (that was inconsistent with section 107(d)). CEQ also declines to require narrow purpose and need statements that would limit reasonable alternatives, preserving agency discretion in defining purpose and need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives analysis as the 'heart' of the EIS
rubrics_metrics.description: §1502.14 reinstates the 1978 language that the alternatives analysis 'is the heart of the environmental impact statement' and revises text to require identification of 'reasonably foreseeable environmental effects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The alternatives analysis should sharply define issues for decision makers and the public and provide a clear basis for choice among alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous and objective evaluation of reasonable alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: §1502.14(a) restores the requirement that agencies must 'rigorously explore and objectively evaluate' reasonable alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ reinstated this language to ensure robust analysis rather than cursory, box-checking analyses. Some commenters expressed litigation concerns, but CEQ concluded the language is necessary to ensure meaningful alternatives analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of alternatives — reasonable range and jurisdictional discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies need not consider every conceivable alternative but must consider a reasonable range of alternatives that fosters informed decision making; agencies have discretion to consider reasonable alternatives not within their jurisdiction but generally are not required to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ replaced prior text limiting number of alternatives with language emphasizing reasonable range. While alternatives outside agency authority may be relevant in programmatic contexts or when funding/authorization is anticipated, an agency is generally not required to analyze alternatives it cannot implement.
